**Where we are ahead:** the only permissively licensed (MIT), no-libc, allocation-free DNP3 that runs with no runtime: unlike opendnp3 (EOL) it is maintained, unlike stepfunc it can be used commercially; the only Zig implementation; SAv2 symmetric g120 codecs are present; outstation behaviour (SBO bound to the arming peer, event ring, fragmentation) is tested against opendnp3 demos. **Where we are behind:** Secure Authentication only symmetric and only in the outstation (no master side), no file transfer/data sets/device attributes, no channel handling (TCP/serial/TLS is the caller's, by design, see *What is deliberately not done*; the rest is in *Backlog / deferred*).


## Design & invariants

Six allocation-free layers, all offline-testable, mirroring IEEE 1815-2012's own layering:

- `link` (§9): the fixed 0x0564 frame. `length` (octet 2) = `5 + user_data.len`, excluding every
  CRC octet. The header block (10 octets: start x2 + length + control + dest + src + CRC) is
  followed by user data split into ≤16-octet blocks, each with its own trailing CRC-16. `Control`
  is a plain struct with explicit bit-shift `toByte`/`fromByte` (not a `packed struct`) so the wire
  layout doesn't depend on Zig's bitfield-packing rules.
- `transport` (§8): one octet (FIN/FIR + 6-bit sequence) per link-frame-sized chunk. `Segmenter`
  produces chunks of up to `link.max_user_data_len - 1` bytes; `Reassembler` enforces that every
  non-FIR segment's sequence is the previous + 1 (mod 64), and that a fresh FIR segment always
  restarts reassembly (discarding any in-flight partial fragment), matching §8.2.3.
- `application` (§4/§5): a 2-byte request header (control + function) or 4-byte response header
  (control + function + IIN1 + IIN2). `FunctionCode` is a non-exhaustive `enum(u8)` — unknown wire
  bytes decode, they just don't match a named tag.
- `objects`: object-header framing (group + variation + qualifier byte [prefix nibble + range
  nibble] + a range field whose width/shape depends on the range nibble) plus the core object
  library. The qualifier/range API is deliberately explicit — the caller states the qualifier it
  wants; `encodeObjectHeader` does not auto-pick the smallest encoding. The shared 1-byte `Flags`
  type documents which bits are always the same across groups (ONLINE/RESTART/COMM_LOST/
  REMOTE_FORCED/LOCAL_FORCED) versus group-specific (bit 5, bit 7) rather than pretending
  certainty on nomenclature this implementation isn't set up to test group-by-group.

- `records`: a table-driven codec for the object *records* that follow an object header. A
  group/variation is described by a `Layout` — `{ flags: bool, value: ValueShape, time: TimeShape }`
  — and one `encode`/`decode` pair handles all of them. This is what makes the outstation's ~40
  group/variation pairs tractable: adding a variation is one table row, not a new struct. The
  binary and double-bit families carry their state *inside* the flags octet (bit 7, bits 6-7), and
  `encode` merges the state into the flags for the caller so it cannot be forgotten. Packed
  single-bit (g1v1, g10v1) and packed double-bit (g3v1) shapes are refused by the record codec and
  handled by explicit `setPackedBit`/`setPackedDoubleBit` helpers, because their size depends on the
  range rather than on the variation.
- `outstation`: the responder. `Outstation.handle(request, now_ms, out) -> ?Reply` is a pure
  function from one application fragment to one application fragment over a caller-owned
  `Database` (seven slices of point structs) and a caller-owned `EventBuffer`;
  `handleFrom(request, peer, now_ms, out)` is the same call with the requesting station's data-link
  address, which is what binds a SELECT to its peer. `Session` composes it with
  `transport.Reassembler`/`Segmenter` and `link` so a caller can feed whole frames, and it is the
  layer that knows the peer, so it calls `handleFrom`.
  `Session` frames all three outbound directions — `feedFrame` (a reply to a request),
  `nextFrames` (the continuation of a multi-fragment response) and `unsolicitedFrames` (an
  outstation-initiated unsolicited response) — because all three share `Session.tx_seq`, and a
  caller that frames an outstation-initiated fragment itself has to duplicate that sequence
  bookkeeping. The fragment-level `Outstation.unsolicited` stays for callers that own their own
  framing.
  Everything time-dependent — the select-before-operate window, the confirm timeout — is driven by
  an injected `now_ms` or by an explicit `confirmTimedOut()` call; the module owns no clock and
  spawns no thread.
- `secure_auth`: opt-in Secure Authentication for the outstation (see "Secure Authentication
  integration" below). `Outstation.handleFrom` hands every request fragment to an attached
  `SecureAuth` before dispatching it; the answer is `pass` (dispatch as before), `silent`, an
  AUTHENTICATE_RESPONSE fragment, or `execute` (dispatch an authenticated request). With no
  `SecureAuth` attached the hook is never entered.

Concurrency: `.reentrant` for the codecs — every type (`Segmenter`, `Reassembler`,
`FrameReceiver`, `records`) is caller-owned with no shared/global state; `Outstation`/`Session` are
`.single_owner` (they hold session state: IIN bits, event buffer, select arm, fragmentation
cursor). Error policy: malformed/short/corrupt bytes never panic in `link`/`transport`/
`application`/`objects`/`records` — every decode path returns a typed error — and the outstation
never returns an error for anything a *peer* got wrong: a hostile request becomes a response with
the appropriate IIN bits (`PARAMETER_ERROR`, `OBJECT_UNKNOWN`, `FUNC_NOT_SUPPORTED`) or a command
echo with a non-success `CommandStatus`. The only error `handle` can return is `BufferTooSmall`,
which is a local programming mistake.

## Outstation behaviour worth pinning down

- **Restart IIN.** Set at construction and after every honoured restart. Cleared *only* by an
  explicit WRITE of g80v1 index 7 with the bit clear (§5.1.4.1) — a master that never clears it
  keeps being told, which is the point.
- **Events are retired on CONFIRM, not on send.** A response carrying events sets CON; the events
  stay in the buffer, marked in-flight, until the master's CONFIRM arrives. `confirmTimedOut()`
  un-marks them so the next poll offers the same ones again. Overflow drops the *oldest* and
  latches IIN2.3 until the buffer drains completely.
- **Fragmentation.** Each fragment of a multi-fragment response carries the *next* application
  sequence number (§5.1.6.2) and clears FIR after the first. Reusing the request's sequence for
  every fragment is a classic interop failure (opendnp3 stalls with "Response with bad sequence").
- **Select-before-operate.** The SELECT is stored with its arm time, its object bytes verbatim and
  the peer that sent it. An OPERATE must carry the SELECT's sequence + 1, byte-identical objects
  and the same peer; otherwise it is `NO_SELECT`. Once the arm window closes the select is dropped
  and the *next* OPERATE is answered `TIMEOUT` rather than `NO_SELECT`, so the master can tell the
  two apart — but a *wrong-peer* OPERATE is `NO_SELECT`, never `TIMEOUT`: no window of that peer's
  closed, and `TIMEOUT` would tell a foreign station that somebody else holds an arm. The
  wrong-peer case is also the one refusal that does **not** consume the arm, so it cannot be used
  to cancel another station's select.
- **Analog deadbands (g34).** `AnalogInput.deadband` (default 0) is the reporting threshold: `reportChange`
  drops a change of an analog input unless it moved more than the deadband from the value last reported
  (`reported`, initially none, so the first change always counts); exactly the deadband is inside it. READ of g34
  (variation 0, 1, 2 or 3, all values, start-stop or count) returns the deadbands of the analog inputs, v1 (16-bit) when
  every value of the range is a whole number below 65536, v2 (32-bit) up to 2^32-1, else v3 (single float)
  when the master asks for variation 0. WRITE of g34 (start-stop, or 1/2-octet index prefix with count) sets them; an index
  past the end, a negative or NaN value or a short body is IIN2.2 PARAMETER_ERROR for that object and the write
  stops there. Analog outputs, counters and the other kinds have no deadband here (a counter's threshold is g21/g22
  territory, not built).
- **Relative-time events (g2v3, g4v3 and the other `rel16` variations).** A point whose
  `event_variation` selects a relative-time variation is reported with a 16-bit millisecond offset from a
  g51 common time-of-occurrence object that precedes it in the fragment (IEEE 1815-2012 Part 4 §4.2.2):
  g51v1 while the clock is synchronised, g51v2 while IIN1.4 NEED_TIME is set. The first such event of an
  emit call sets the CTO to its own time; a later event earlier than the CTO or more than 65535 ms after it
  starts a new g51. (Before, a relative variation was written with offset 0 and no g51, which no master
  can place in time.)
- **Link-layer confirmed delivery (`link_session.zig`).** Receive side, always on: RESET_LINK_STATES
  is ACKed and sets the expected frame-count bit to 1; CONFIRMED_USER_DATA with FCV set and the expected
  FCB is delivered, ACKed and flips the expectation; the other FCB is a repeat of a delivered frame (its
  ACK was lost) and is ACKed without being delivered or executed again; a confirmed frame before a reset,
  or without FCV, or a TEST_LINK_STATES out of count, is NACKed (IEC 60870-5-2 two-state scheme, 1815-2012
  §9.2.6). A broadcast is never confirmed (delivered as unconfirmed, no reply). Send side, opt-in
  (`Config.link_confirms`, default off like opendnp3 and Step Function I/O): the response goes out as
  RESET_LINK_STATES, then one CONFIRMED_USER_DATA frame per link ACK with alternating FCB (`link_session.Primary`),
  retransmitted unchanged after `link_response_timeout_ms` (default 1000) up to `link_retries` (3) times
  (`Session.pollLink` / `nextLinkDeadline`); a NACK or the last timeout drops the fragment and un-resets the link.
  The same pair serves the master (`dir = true`).
- **Link direction.** §9.2.4.1.2's DIR bit is 1 for master-originated frames and 0 for
  outstation-originated ones. `Session` sends 0. Getting this backwards makes a real master drop
  every reply as "master frame received for master".

## Master session (`master.zig`)

The master is a pure state machine like the outstation: allocation-free, no timer, no I/O; the caller passes
`now_ms` (milliseconds since the UNIX epoch, the clock the outstation stamps events with), asks `poll` for
the next request, feeds each received application fragment to `handle`, and sleeps until `nextWakeup`.
`master.Session` adds the transport and link framing (requests as unconfirmed user data with DIR = 1; the
receive side ACKs confirmed user data from an outstation that sends it, with the frame-count rule of
`link_session`). Modelled on opendnp3's master and Step Function I/O's, behaviour only.

- **Tasks and priority** (lowest first): command, clear restart, disable unsolicited, delay measure, write
  time, integrity poll, enable unsolicited, class 1/2/3 poll. One request is outstanding at a time.
- **Startup** (the opendnp3 order): DISABLE_UNSOLICITED (g60v2-v4), integrity poll (g60v2, v3, v4, v1), then
  ENABLE_UNSOLICITED; each part can be switched off in `Config`. `integrity_poll_ms` and `class_poll_ms`
  repeat the polls.
- **IIN-driven**: device restart -> WRITE g80v1 index 7 = 0 (`clear_restart_iin`); class 1/2/3 events -> a class
  poll (`scan_on_event_iin`); NEED_TIME -> `time_sync`: `lan` writes g50v1 with `now_ms`, `non_lan` sends
  DELAY_MEASURE first and writes `now_ms + delay/2` (g52v2 carries the outstation's turnaround).
- **Commands**: `queueCommand` (bounded, 8) with a CROB (g12v1) or an analog output block (g41v1-v4) at a 1- or
  2-octet index; direct operate, or SELECT then OPERATE at the next sequence number once the SELECT echoed
  success. `Event.command_done` carries the outstation's echo status (`format_error` for a response that does
  not echo the command, `timeout` when none came). A command is never retried by the master: the
  outstation may already have acted.
- **CONFIRM**: every response and unsolicited response with CON gets a CONFIRM carrying its sequence number
  (UNS set for an unsolicited one); every fragment of a multi-fragment response is confirmed and the next one
  must carry the next sequence number. A response with a wrong sequence number, FIR missing on the first
  fragment, or while nothing is outstanding is ignored.
- **Unsolicited**: delivered as `Data{ .unsolicited = true }`; a repeat with the sequence number of the
  previous one is confirmed again and not delivered twice (opendnp3 does the same).
- **Timeouts**: no complete response within `response_timeout_ms` fails the task. A poll or other task is
  retried after `task_retry_ms`, `max_task_retries` times, then `task_done{ ok = false }`; a periodic task keeps its
  schedule. IIN bits seen on any response are acted on at once.
- **Reading the data**: `Data.measurements()` walks the objects: static and event binary, double-bit, binary
  output, counter, frozen counter, analog input and output, with start-stop ranges and index prefixes,
  packed bit forms, g51 common times resolving relative-time events. Any other object (and any
  truncation) stops the walk with `ok = false`; the module never panics on hostile bytes.
- **Not done**: one outstation per `Master` (a second association is a second `Master`); no
  Secure Authentication on the master side (SPEC *Backlog*); file transfer, data sets, device attributes, octet
  strings and the other groups listed under *What is deliberately not done* are not decoded.

## CRC verification

DNP3's link-layer CRC-16 is the reveng CRC-catalogue "CRC-16/DNP": width=16, poly=0x3D65,
init=0x0000, refin=true, refout=true, xorout=0xFFFF, check("123456789")=0xEA82. `link.crc16`
delegates to `std.hash.crc.@"CRC-16/DNP"` (std builds its table from the reflected polynomial
0xA6BC = `reflect(0x3D65, 16)`).

`link.zig`'s tests pin the catalogue check value and further vectors (empty input, single bytes
0x00/0xFF, short ASCII strings, a 16-byte sequential block, a 16-byte repeated block, and two
synthetic 8/13-byte link-header-shaped blocks) computed by a from-scratch bit-serial engine written
directly from the (width, poly, init, refin, refout, xorout) parameters, independent of any table
code. `src/goldens.zig` replays real link frames from live opendnp3 sessions (see Verification):
opendnp3 built and validated the CRC on every frame this module sent, and this module validated
the CRC on every frame opendnp3 sent, in both roles. Wireshark's DNP3 dissector also parsed all
captured frames without a CRC or malformed indication.

The full-stack round-trip tests in `link.zig`/`root.zig` are self-consistency tests (encode with
this module, decode with this module, assert equality) and are documented as such.

## Threat model / out of scope

DNP3 (outside Secure Authentication) is an unauthenticated, unencrypted field protocol by design —
this module's job is robustness, not confidentiality/integrity against an active attacker. Hostile
or corrupt bytes from a misbehaving device or a MITM resolve to typed errors, never panics or
out-of-bounds reads, across every decode entry point (`link.decodeFrame`,
`transport.Reassembler.feed`, `application.decodeRequestHeader`/`decodeResponseHeader`,
`objects.decodeObjectHeader`, every `gNN.VN.decode`).

The outstation widens the attack surface, so its entry points get the same treatment: a request
fragment that is not FIR+FIN, an object header whose range is inverted or empty, a range or count
that runs past the database, a count that overruns the fragment, a start/stop range spanning the
whole 32-bit space, a prefix-less command header naming a point index past the 16-bit index space,
a variation the module does not implement, an unassigned function code, and a zero-length fragment
all resolve to a response with the right IIN bits rather than an error or a crash.

The threat model also covers WELL-FORMED requests. A `READ g20v2` -- a spec-defined 16-bit
counter variation -- against a counter holding more than `0xFFFF` must not drive an unbounded
series of identical empty fragments (the value the master asked for cannot be carried in the
variation it asked for; the response cursor must not treat that as "no room, retry"); a
`READ g30v1` against a point CONFIGURED as a float must not reach an inactive union field; and a
`DIRECT_OPERATE` carrying a NaN setpoint must not walk through a declared `[min, max]`
(`value < min or value > max` is false for a NaN). The threat model is not "malformed bytes": it is
every request a master can legally send, against every state the caller's database can legally
hold. Wire-driven
object-instance counts always go through `objects.Range.objectCount()` / `objectSpanBytes()`, whose
arithmetic is widened to `u64`; a raw `stop - start + 1` on a wire value is a defect, and an index
that does not fit the 16-bit point space is refused, never truncated onto a different point.

`Session.feedFrame` filters on **both** data-link addresses. A frame addressed to another station is
dropped without being decoded further, and the three IEEE 1815 broadcast addresses (0xFFFD-0xFFFF)
are executed but never answered. A frame whose *source* is not `config.master_address` is dropped
too, and that test has no broadcast exemption: one `Outstation` is one DNP3 association — the
logical connection between one master and one outstation, identified by the set of addresses it
uses — so a frame from any other source belongs to a different association. `require_master_source`
turns the source filter off for the same reason opendnp3 offers `respondToAnySource` and Step
Function I/O's `dnp3` offers `respond_to_any_master`; like both of those it defaults to on.

The select-before-operate arm is bound to the peer independently of that switch. `Select` records
the source address the SELECT arrived from, and an OPERATE from any other address is `NO_SELECT`
and does not disarm what it failed to fire — so on a link carrying more than one master-capable
station, one station cannot ride or cancel another's arm. `Outstation.handleFrom(request, peer, …)`
is how the peer reaches the outstation; `Outstation.handle(request, …)` is the same call with no
peer named, and "no peer" is a distinct value rather than a wildcard — it matches only itself, so
mixing the two entry points across a SELECT/OPERATE pair is refused rather than waved through.

Neither filter is authentication: a source address is an addressing field, not a credential, and
authorising the peer remains the caller's job (or DNP3-SA's). Serving several masters properly
means one `Outstation` per association over a shared point database, which is what both reference
stacks do.

With `secure_auth` attached, critical requests are authenticated before they run: a failed
authentication never executes the request, the outstanding challenge is consumed by any reply
(good or bad) so a failed attempt leaves nothing a replay could use, every MAC comparison is the
constant-time one in `sa.mac`, and challenge / aggressive-mode sequence numbers only move forward.

Four fuzz harnesses back this: two 20 000-iteration loops over uniformly random bytes (application
fragments, link frames through a `Session`), and two over *structured* draws — function code,
group/variation, qualifier, and range fields drawn from the boundary values of each field's
representable range, which is the only way a fragment ever reaches the command path's range
arithmetic. The structured loops assert they produced those shapes, so a generator that stops
reaching them fails rather than reading green. `std.testing.fuzz` targets over the same generator
(`Outstation.handle`, `Session.feedFrame`) hand the shape space to the real fuzzer.

Out of scope: unsolicited *retry* policy of the outstation (the fragment builder is here, the timer is
the caller's), file-transfer objects (g70), data-set objects (g85-g88), device attributes (g0), octet
strings (g110/g111), time-and-interval (g50v4), analog deadbands (g34), Secure Authentication beyond the
outstation's symmetric procedures (see its own section), and any actual transport (TCP/serial) I/O — this
module hands the caller bytes to send/receive, nothing more. The reasons and the open items are in *What is
deliberately not done* and *Backlog / deferred*.

## g120 Secure Authentication — SAv2 symmetric core

`sa.zig` implements the SAv2 symmetric authentication of IEEE 1815-2012 §7 / IEC 62351-5 over
object group 120:

- **AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394)** — via the shared `modules/aeskw` module (`aeskw.wrap`/`aeskw.unwrap`
  over `std.crypto.core.aes`, AES-128 and AES-256 KEK; std ships no key-wrap). Byte-exact against
  the RFC 3394 §4 published vectors. The module is shared with `jwe` and `xmlenc`.
- **MAC algorithms** (`mac`) — the SA algorithm registry: HMAC-SHA-1 (truncated to 4/8/10 octets),
  HMAC-SHA-256 (truncated to 8/16 octets), and AES-GMAC (12-octet tag), with
  constant-time verification (`ctEql` in `sa.zig`). HMAC runs on `std.crypto`, GMAC on the
  shared `modules/aesgcm` module (std AES-GCM is 2.6x slower on Zig 0.17, #36256).
- **g120 codecs** — `Challenge` (v1), `Reply` (v2), `AggressiveModeRequest` (v3),
  `SessionKeyStatusRequest` (v4), `SessionKeyStatus` (v5), `SessionKeyChange` (v6), `SaError` (v7),
  `AggregateMac` (v9), plus the group-120 free-format object header (qualifier `0x5B`).
- **Flow + state** — `computeReplyMac`/`verifyReplyMac` (challenge-response MAC input),
  `wrapSessionKeys`/`unwrapSessionKeys`, and `SeqCounter` / `KeyExpiry` / `lookupUpdateKey` state
  helpers that take the clock/counters as parameters (no wall-clock dependence).


**MAC-input construction (security crux):** the reply MAC is computed over the received challenge
message concatenated with the critical ASDU being authenticated; callers pass the exact wire byte
slices and both sides must agree on their definition. This follows the §7 description and is
validated for full-flow self-consistency (build→verify accept; flip one byte of the MAC or of the
authenticated ASDU → reject). It is **not** validated against a live opendnp3 golden MAC vector
(modern opendnp3 dropped its SA implementation), so wire-level MAC interop remains unproven; the
primitives underneath (AES-KW, HMAC truncation, GMAC) are KAT-exact.

**Out of scope:** the SAv5/SAv6 asymmetric update-key change (g120 v8/v10–v15: RSA/DSA-signed
remote update-key change, user certificates, user-status change), and the DNP3-specific AES-GMAC IV
derivation (the GMAC primitive is provided and KAT-validated; the caller supplies the 12-octet IV).

## Secure Authentication integration (outstation)

`secure_auth.zig` drives the IEEE 1815-2012 §7 (SAv5) **symmetric** procedures on the outstation
side over the `sa.zig` codecs. It is opt-in (`Outstation.setSecureAuth`) and holds bounded state
only: one outstanding challenge, one key-change window, one stored critical request in
caller-owned storage. It is clock-injected (the outstation's `now_ms`) and takes its challenge
randomness from a caller `RandomSource`. It does no I/O and no allocation.

**Reference check.** The owner rule asks for the reference's behaviour first. The reference
(opendnp3) dropped SA from its current releases and there is no SA-capable peer in this
repository. The behaviour below is therefore read from the standard's procedure as the `sa.zig`
codecs encode it, and each choice that could differ from a foreign implementation is listed as
an open question in the Backlog. Wire interop with a foreign SA master is **unproven**.


Behaviour, and why:

- **Critical requests** (`Config.critical`, a 256-bit `FunctionSet`; default
  `FunctionSet.default_critical` = WRITE, SELECT, OPERATE, DIRECT_OPERATE(+NR), COLD/WARM_RESTART,
  INITIALIZE_DATA/APPLICATION, START/STOP_APPLICATION, SAVE_CONFIGURATION, ENABLE/
  DISABLE_UNSOLICITED, ASSIGN_CLASS, OPEN/CLOSE/DELETE_FILE, ACTIVATE_CONFIG). These are the
  requests that change outputs, configuration or running state. READ, CONFIRM, the freezes,
  DELAY_MEASURE and RECORD_CURRENT_TIME are left out, as the optional rows of the standard's
  critical-function table. The caller overrides the set with `with`/`without`.
- **Challenge**: a critical request is stored, not run. The answer is AUTHENTICATE_RESPONSE (0x83,
  FIR+FIN, no CON) carrying g120v1: CSQ = previous + 1, user `Config.challenge_user` (default 1,
  the standard's default user), the configured MAC algorithm (default HMAC-SHA-256/16, the
  standard's default for networked links), reason CRITICAL, and `challenge_len` random octets
  (default 4, the standard's minimum; clamped to 4..64). The whole fragment is kept as the
  "challenge message".
- **Reply** (AUTHENTICATE_REQUEST g120v2): accepted only if the CSQ is the outstanding one, the
  application sequence number is the challenged request's own (the exchange consumes no
  sequence number, so an authenticated SELECT is still followed by an OPERATE with seq + 1), the
  peer is the one that sent the request, the user has installed and unexpired session keys, and
  `sa.verifyReplyMac` (constant time, control-direction key, MAC over `challenge message ‖
  critical request`) passes. A reply that names the outstanding exchange (its CSQ, sequence number
  and peer) consumes it, whether its MAC verifies or not; one that does not is ignored and leaves
  the challenge in place. A new critical request replaces an outstanding challenge (one at a
  time), and a reply after `reply_timeout_ms` (default 2 s) finds none.
- **No-ack critical requests** (DIRECT_OPERATE_NR, the *_NR freezes) cannot be challenged, because
  the master expects no answer. They are discarded unless sent in aggressive mode.
- **Aggressive mode**: a request whose first object is g120v3 and whose last object is g120v9
  (its size fixed by the MAC algorithm) is verified in one step: CSQ = last CSQ + 1, a challenge
  has been sent before, user keyed, MAC over `last challenge message ‖ request up to the g120v9
  object` in constant time. Success executes the objects between them, advances the CSQ (so the
  same message cannot pass twice) and cancels any outstanding challenge.
- **Session keys**: g120v4 is answered with g120v5 (KSQ = previous + 1, the user's key status,
  configured key-wrap and MAC algorithms, fresh challenge data, no MAC). Every g120v5 opens the
  single key-change window for that user and KSQ. g120v6 is accepted only inside it with the same
  KSQ and user, an update key of the length the key-wrap algorithm requires, AES-KW integrity, and
  the SAv5 layout bound to that window's status (`sa.unwrapSessionKeysWithStatus`, see "Key-wrap
  layout" below). The new keys replace the old ones, which are wiped. The
  confirmation is a g120v5 with status OK whose MAC is computed under the new monitoring-direction
  key over the received g120v6 object. A refused change is answered with a g120v5 with status
  AUTH_FAIL and leaves the user's existing keys as they were.
- **Expiry**: keys are invalidated (wiped, status COMM_FAIL) after `session_key_timeout_ms`
  (default 30 min) or `session_key_max_messages` (default 2000). Both defaults are twice the
  standard's expected change interval and count. A zero limit disables that axis.
- **Errors**: every authentication failure is answered with a g120v7, code 1 (authentication
  failed), until `max_error_messages` (default 2) have gone out. `sa.ErrorCode` follows the
  IEEE 1815-2012 error-code table as opendnp3's `AuthErrorCode` (Apache-2.0) numbers it: 1
  authentication failed, 4 aggressive mode unsupported, 5 MAC algorithm not supported, 6 key-wrap
  algorithm not supported, 7 authorization failed, 8 update-key method not permitted, 9 invalid
  signature, 10 invalid certification data, 11 unknown user, 12 max session-key-status requests
  exceeded; a value outside it is kept raw. After that the outstation is
  silent until a successful key change resets the budget. A master's own g120v7
  (AUTHENTICATE_REQUEST_NO_ACK) is counted and not answered. Unexpected or undecodable
  AUTHENTICATE_REQUESTs are counted and ignored.
- **Statistics** (`Statistics`) count each of these events in memory, and READ of g121 (variation 0 or 1; all,
  start-stop or count) returns them on the wire as the 18 security statistics, in the index order of
  opendnp3's `SecurityStatIndex` (0 unexpected messages ... 17 rekeys due to restart) with the layout of its
  `Group121Var1`: flags (ONLINE), association id (`Config.association_id`), 32-bit count, little-endian.
  Statistics the outstation has no concept of (1 authorization failures, 4 and 17 rekeys, 7 critical
  messages sent, 15 and 16 update-key changes) read 0; 5/6 count every response sent and request screened
  while SA is attached; 8 counts the requests it challenged or took in aggressive mode. They are not
  part of the class 0 scan and no g122 events are generated (the g121/g122 codecs are in `objects`).

**Key-wrap layout.** The g120v6 wrapped data is
AES-KW (RFC 3394) over: key length (u16 LE), control key, monitoring key, the key-status message,
and zero padding to a multiple of 8. The key-status message is the g120v5 object body that opened
the key-change window, exactly as sent: KSQ through the challenge data, plus its MAC when it had
one, without the 6-octet g120 object header. `sa.wrapSessionKeysWithStatus` /
`sa.unwrapSessionKeysWithStatus` implement it. The unwrap compares the embedded status in
constant time (`ctEql` over exactly the expected status's length). Every wire-dependent failure
returns the one error `Unauthentic`: integrity, length field, total length, or a different status.

Why: the KSQ alone cannot stop a replay. It restarts at 0 with the outstation, and any peer can
step it with unauthenticated g120v4s. Binding the change to the status's fresh random challenge
data closes the replay of a recorded g120v6 after a restart (regression test in
`secure_auth`). The layout is the one recalled for IEEE 1815-2012 SAv5 and opendnp3 2.x; it is
**not checked against the standard's text** or a foreign implementation. Which bytes count as
"the key-status message" (object body, whole object, or ASDU) and the padding byte are the
uncertain parts.

Padding contents are deliberately not checked, because another implementation may pad
differently. The layout carries no status length of its own. So an expected status that is a
strict prefix of the wrapped one, and pads to the same total, compares equal on the bytes it
has. That is enough for the binding: the expected status is always the outstation's own, exact
and fresh, so any extra bytes are padding to it.

An expected status shorter than a minimal g120v5 body (`sa.min_wrapped_status_len` = 11-octet
fixed part + 4 octets of challenge data) is refused with the same `Unauthentic`: it would bind
the change to nothing.

The older `sa.wrapSessionKeys` / `unwrapSessionKeys` pair stays as a public codec. Its keys-only
layout is not what SAv5 outstations use.

*Constant time (ctgrind target `keys5`).* After AES-KW has authenticated the plaintext, the unwrap
declassifies exactly two public byte ranges (`makeMemDefined`, a no-op without `-fvalgrind`):
- the 2-octet length field, `recovered[0..2]`;
- the embedded status, `recovered[2+2·klen .. 2+2·klen+expected.len]`, which went out on the wire
  as the g120v5.

The keys stay tainted. Native (skylake):
- tainted in-file 6. All six are `aeskw` root.zig, the timing-safe integrity verdict, once
  per unwrap call site in the harness (genuine, tampered, other status) × 16/32-octet keys.
- No context fires in `sa.zig` itself.
- control 0; trap 0.

x86_64 portable:
- tainted in-file 121, identical to `keys`.
- control 4: printing, Writer.zig–1945.
- trap 61, histogram:
  - sa.zig ×16 and sa.zig ×8 (the status `ctEql`);
  - sa.zig ×4 each (the length checks);
  - aeskw root.zig ×6;
  - Writer.zig ×12;
  - memcpy.zig ×11.

Nothing is tainted in the trap build. Those contexts are std's bitsliced soft AES padding a
partial batch with `undefined` lanes, and that definedness reaching plaintext that is public
after the verdict. The declassification above is compiled out in that build.

**Security notes** (from the independent review):

- *Unauthenticated messages can disturb an exchange in flight.* SA cannot
  stop a station from sending unauthenticated traffic. Each such message can cost the master one
  exchange, and the master recovers with its next attempt:
  - another critical request replaces the outstanding challenge;
  - a reply with the right CSQ, sequence and peer but a bad MAC consumes it;
  - a g120v4 or a junk g120v6 closes or replaces the key-change window;
  - a critical request also advances the CSQ and the "last challenge" an aggressive-mode master
    chains from.

  An on-path attacker can do the same by dropping frames, and the link-layer source filter
  (`require_master_source`, on by default) already keeps other stations' frames out. The one
  cheap narrowing is in place: a reply that does not name the outstanding exchange (another CSQ,
  sequence number or peer) is ignored without consuming it. It cannot pass, so ignoring it opens
  no replay.
- *Status requests do not enumerate users.* A g120v4 for an unknown user is answered like one for a
  known user without keys (NOT_INIT), and that window refuses every key change. Timing still
  differs (no MAC is computed for an unknown or unkeyed user); user numbers are not secret.

- *A request SA only challenges, refuses or ignores does not touch the outstation.*
  The screen runs before the outstation abandons a response series, clears the await-confirm
  state or records the sequence number, so an unauthenticated critical request does not abort a
  multi-fragment response or an event report awaiting its CONFIRM.
- *Unauthenticated state changes that remain (documented).* CONFIRM is not critical
  (as in the standard), so a forged CONFIRM retires the events in flight. IMMEDIATE_FREEZE and
  FREEZE_CLEAR are optional-critical and left out of the default set. A caller who needs them
  authenticated adds them with `FunctionSet.with`. CONFIRM cannot usefully be challenged.
- *Aggressive-mode age and online guessing (documented).* An aggressive-mode request
  stays valid until the CSQ or the last challenge moves on, or the keys expire, so a withheld
  request can be delivered late. The standard has the same property and adds no timeout either.
  There is also no per-user lockout after repeated MAC failures: the g120v7 replies stop after
  `max_error_messages`, but verification continues. With the default 16-octet MAC that is moot.
  With the 4- or 8-octet truncations it leaves online guessing unthrottled. Candidates: a
  maximum age measured from the last challenge, and invalidating a user's keys after N failures
  (the standard's maximum-authentication-failures statistic).

**Anchoring.** No live SA peer exists, so the first `secure_auth` test pins a whole exchange
against vectors **derived by hand outside the module**: Python's `hmac`/`hashlib` for every MAC
and the `cryptography` package's RFC 3394 wrap for the g120v6 payload, over the byte layouts
above. The exchange is key status, key change and confirmation MAC, challenge, reply, then
aggressive mode. These vectors prove the module computes what this section says, not that a
foreign SA master computes the same.

## Verification

- **Run:** `scripts/modtest dnp3` (the same suite as `zig build test-dnp3`, optionally with
  `-Doptimize=ReleaseFast`). Offline: the interop captures are in-tree goldens, no peer is needed.
- **Test classes by area.** `link`: CRC catalogue check value and known-answer vectors, control-octet
  round-trip, frame round-trips (empty, short, multi-block, exact 16-octet block boundary), encode/decode
  error paths and a malformed-input sweep. `transport`: octet round-trip, segmentation and reassembly
  (empty, single, multi-segment), sequence-mismatch, continuation-before-FIR, FIR-restart, buffer-too-small
  and empty-segment errors. `application`: control and IIN round-trips, request/response headers,
  `buildRequest`, short-fragment errors, non-exhaustive function-code decode. `objects`: qualifier byte,
  object-header round-trips for every range shape, range/qualifier mismatch errors, short/garbage sweeps,
  flags byte, and a round-trip of every core object. `records`: the layout table's wire lengths against
  the object library, state-in-flags for binary and double-bit, absolute-time and float variations,
  narrow-variation range rejection, packed shapes, the point-kind to group mapping. `root`: full
  link-transport-application round-trips (single and forced multi-frame) in both roles.
  `sa`: AES-KW RFC 3394 vectors through the shared `aeskw` module (which carries its own KAT suite),
  HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 4231) and HMAC-SHA-1 (RFC 2202) truncation KATs, AES-GMAC (McGrew GCM test case 1),
  constant-time verify accept/tamper/wrong-length, g120 codec round-trips and garbage sweeps, session-key
  wrap/unwrap including the SAv5 status-bound layout (every wire failure is one error, length-field lies,
  the minimum status), the challenge-response flow, and the `SeqCounter`/`KeyExpiry`/`lookupUpdateKey`
  helpers. `outstation`: IIN bits, READ (class 0 over all seven point types, every qualifier shape,
  variation 0, packed variations, mixed-variation header splitting, hostile ranges), events (ordering,
  confirm retires, timeout releases, per-class filtering, ring overflow), commands (SELECT+OPERATE,
  timeout, wrong sequence/objects/index/peer, DIRECT_OPERATE and its no-ack form, every CROB operation,
  analog output bounds, hook veto), DELAY_MEASURE, restart, unsolicited enable/disable and responses,
  freeze and freeze-clear, ASSIGN_CLASS, fragmentation, hostile input (including a full-width command
  range and a point index past the 16-bit space), and `Session` (link-service replies, both address
  filters and the source-filter opt-out, SELECT/OPERATE across stations in both directions, broadcast
  executed but unanswered, a request split across transport segments, out-of-order segments, bad CRC,
  `unsolicitedFrames` framing and `tx_seq`). `secure_auth`: the hand-derived exchange vectors, bad reply
  MAC and its retry, replies with the wrong CSQ / sequence / peer / user / key, reply timeout and
  replaced challenges, SELECT+OPERATE each authenticated, non-critical requests byte-identical with and
  without SA, the critical-set override, no-ack requests, aggressive-mode refusals, key-change refusals
  (KSQ, user, update key, short data, replay including a recorded key change replayed after a restart),
  expiry by time / count / status request, wiped old keys, the error budget, challenge shapes and the
  storage boundary, and a challenged request leaving a response awaiting its confirm alone.
- **Goldens and oracles.** `src/goldens.zig` replays sessions captured from a live **opendnp3** peer
  (Apache-2.0, built from source, used strictly as a black box): (1) its `master-demo` against this
  outstation over a real loopback TCP socket with a byte-moving proxy in between: startup tasks, an
  integrity scan (class 3/2/1/0), an ad-hoc `ScanRange(g1v2, 0, 3)`, DISABLE_UNSOLICITED, a CROB
  select+operate that opendnp3 reported as SUCCESS, a class-1 exception scan across an injected
  process-image change (a g11v2 and a g2v2 event, CONFIRMed), a COLD_RESTART, and a second integrity scan
  after the master cleared the restart IIN with a WRITE of g80v1; (2) the same master against a
  fragmented response (300 binary inputs, `max_tx_fragment` 400), which opendnp3 confirmed and
  reassembled with no sequence warnings; (3) the reverse direction, this module's master-side codecs
  parsing what opendnp3's `outstation-demo` encoded (an unsolicited NULL response, g1v2, g20v1, g52v2).
  Replaying (1) and (2) in order reproduces every reply byte for byte, 48-bit event timestamps included,
  because the tests advance the same injected clock the harness did. The captured frames were also
  dissected with Wireshark's DNP3 dissector: no malformed or expert indication, and DIR/PRM, addresses,
  function codes, FIR/FIN/CON/SEQ, the restart and class-1 IIN bits and every object identifier of the
  class-0 response matched this module's decoder. Tests marked SELF-DERIVED prove self-consistency only.
  The first `secure_auth` test pins a whole SA exchange against vectors derived outside the module by
  `tools/sa_outstation_kat.py` (Python `hmac`/`hashlib` and the `cryptography` package's RFC 3394 wrap),
  which proves the module computes what *Secure Authentication integration* says, not that a foreign
  SA master computes the same.
- **Fuzz:** deterministic driver, `DNP3_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`: harness `dnp3-fragment`
  (`Outstation.handle` over structured request fragments), `dnp3-session` (`Session.feedFrame` over
  structured, damaged-genuine and damaged link frames; both in `src/outstation.zig`) and `dnp3-sa` (SA
  wrap, MAC and g120 objects as an oracle, `src/fuzz_test.zig`). Each has a reach test that fails when the
  generator stops producing the shapes it exists for; fixed-iteration random-byte loops and
  `std.testing.fuzz` targets over the same generators sit beside them.
- **ctgrind:** rows `mac`, `keys` and `keys5` in `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv` (SA session key
  through every MAC and the reply MAC; update and session keys through the key wrap; the SAv5
  status-bound wrap), read in *Key-wrap layout*.
- **Stack probe:** `src/stackprobe_test.zig` (ReleaseFast) goes red when an SA entry point outgrows its
  dead-stack burn in `src/burn.zig` or leaves a key in a frame; it covers the MAC paths, the keys-only
  wrap/unwrap and the key-change wrap/unwrap with the key-status message.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **Transport I/O (TCP/serial/TLS).** `Session` consumes and produces byte slices; running it over a
  channel is the caller's job (reference: opendnp3 and stepfunc ship channels, this module is
  allocation-free, clock-free and I/O-free by design).
- **Unsolicited retry policy.** `Outstation.unsolicited` builds the fragment and `confirmTimedOut`
  puts the events back; the retry timer, the back-off and the "unsolicited allowed after the first
  integrity poll" convention are the caller's, because the module owns no clock and no timer.
- **File transfer (g70), device attributes (g0) and data sets (g85-g88).** Their wire formats and
  procedures are in IEEE 1815-2012 Parts 4/5 only (paywalled); opendnp3, the permissively
  licensed reference, lists none of them among its features, and the one implementation that does
  (stepfunc) is source-available under a non-commercial licence that may not be read. Without a
  readable second source a codec here would be a guess that no peer has checked, so they are not built.
- **Octet-string points (g110/g111) in the outstation database, and g50v2.** The object codecs exist
  (`objects.g110`/`g111`, `objects.g50.V4`), but the outstation's point database is a closed set of seven
  fixed-record kinds; an octet-string kind (the variation is the length, so a run has no fixed record
  size) touches the database, class polls and the event buffer. Not built until a user needs it.
- **Several masters on one `Outstation`.** One `Outstation` is one DNP3 association; serving several
  masters means one `Outstation` per association over a shared point database, as both reference
  stacks do.

## Backlog / deferred

- **Secure Authentication, what the outstation integration leaves out:** the SAv5/SAv6
  asymmetric update-key change (g120 v8/v10-v15), the g122 security-statistic *events* (g121 reads
  are served), authenticated responses in the monitoring direction,
  AES-GMAC as the challenge MAC (its IV derivation is out of scope in `sa.zig`), the master
  side.
- **Open questions for the SA integration** (each needs the standard's text or a foreign
  implementation to settle): (a) which bytes count as "the key-status message" in the g120v6
  wrapped data (object body, whole object or ASDU) and the padding byte (the decision itself is in
  *Key-wrap layout*); (b) what the g120v5 MAC covers (here: the received g120v6 object, under the new
  monitoring key, only in the confirmation); (c) the exact default critical-function table;
  (d) whether a reply may carry a sequence number other than the challenged request's; (e) the
  aggressive-mode MAC input (here: last challenge message || request up to g120v9).
- **Portable ctgrind trap counts for `keys5`** include std soft-AES pad-lane definedness
  reaching post-verdict public plaintext (`sa.zig` unwrap); revisit if std stops padding with
  undefined.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** `src/goldens.zig` replays complete data-link frames captured from live TCP sessions with a real opendnp3 3.1.x peer, both directions (each golden is labelled CAPTURED or SELF-DERIVED; the sessions are ordered and stateful, replayed on an injected clock). Secure Authentication has no live foreign peer: `src/secure_auth.zig` pins a whole exchange against vectors derived outside the module by `tools/sa_outstation_kat.py` (see the *Anchoring* paragraph under Secure Authentication). The remaining codec paths are self-tested.
